title: India's ₹99,000-Crore Submarine Deal With Germany Nears Final Signature
excerpt: Project 75(I) for six advanced AIP submarines clears finance ministry; only Cabinet security committee approval remains before India's largest defence contract is signed.
body:
• India's ₹99,000-crore (~$10 billion) Project 75(I) submarine deal with Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems is in its final stages, with contract signing expected by September 2026.
  • The deal covers six advanced diesel-electric submarines with Air-Independent Propulsion (AIP) technology, to be built at Mazagon Dock in Mumbai.
  • An inter-governmental agreement was signed during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to India in January; finance ministry clearance came in May.
  • Only Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approval remains before the contract is signed.

India's largest-ever defence deal is nearing its final signature. The ₹99,000-crore (~$10 billion) Project 75(I) submarine programme — which will see six advanced conventional submarines built at Mumbai's Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MDL) with technology from Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) — has cleared its last financial hurdle and awaits only Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approval.

A Decades-Long Journey

The project traces its origins to a 1999 Cabinet Committee on Security decision for 24 conventional submarines by 2030. Twenty-seven years later, India has just six of those boats — the French-designed Scorpène-class vessels of Project 75, delivered a decade behind schedule.

https://x.com/WarMonitorINTL/status/2088882372892557784

P75(I) was originally conceived as a second production line using Russian designs. It was repurposed in 2007 into a hunt for the most advanced conventional submarine technology available, with Air-Independent Propulsion (AIP) at the top of the requirements list. AIP allows diesel-electric submarines to remain submerged for weeks rather than days — a capability that India's neighbours China and Pakistan already possess.

Germany's Return After the HDW Shadow

The partnership with TKMS carries historical weight. Germany's HDW (now part of TKMS) built India's Shishumar-class submarines in the 1980s, transferring genuine submarine-building expertise to Mazagon Dock. But kickback allegations in 1987 torpedoed the relationship — the fifth and sixth boats were cancelled, and the German yard was blacklisted for years. The charges eventually dissolved without convictions, but so did India's plans for more German boats.

"I am convinced that India will develop into a global center for submarine technology and manufacturing. Our partnership with MDL is based on trust, innovation, and shared goals that go far beyond individual contracts."

— Oliver Burkhard, CEO, ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems

TKMS returned to the competition in 2023, formalizing a joint bid with MDL during German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius's visit. By January 2025, it was the sole compliant bidder after rival Larsen & Toubro's partnership with Spain's Navantia failed the Indian Navy's requirement for a sea-proven AIP system.

What India Is Buying

The submarines will be heavily enlarged hybrids of Germany's U-212CD class. Where the standard boats displace around 2,800 tons, the Indian variant is projected at 3,400–3,500 tons submerged — nearly double the Kalvari-class Scorpènes — with space for a scaled-up AIP plant, bigger batteries, indigenous combat systems, and a vertical launch system for land-attack cruise missiles.

No submarine of this exact configuration has been built before. India deliberately chose a boat that does not yet exist, because helping to design it is precisely the competence New Delhi is trying to acquire.

Timeline and What Remains

The financial roadmap has been settled. In late June, the Indian Navy and TKMS concluded price negotiations at roughly €8 billion. The union finance ministry cleared the deal on May 28. German Defence Minister Pistorius, after hosting Indian counterpart Rajnath Singh in Berlin in April, declared himself "very, very confident" the contract would be signed within three months.

"I think we are a couple of weeks away from the conclusion of the agreement. Of course, it is the decision of the Indian side, it is their purchase."

— Philipp Ackermann, German Ambassador to India

The remaining step is CCS approval. Once signed, the timeline calls for roughly two years of design work before steel is cut, six to seven years to the first submarine, then one boat per year. A late-2026 signature would mean the first submarine commissions around 2033, with the sixth arriving near 2038.

Diaspora Angle

The deal deepens the India-Germany strategic partnership at a time when Berlin is actively pivoting toward the Indo-Pacific. For India's defence industrial base, it represents a generational opportunity to move from licensed assembly to genuine submarine design collaboration — a transition that Indian-origin defence professionals and analysts in the diaspora have long advocated.
